Foundations: What Registration and Compliance Really Mean

Before you fill any form, you need to know what the law expects of a small business in Nigeria and which structure fits you. This module explains the regulators you will meet, the difference between a business name and a limited company under CAMA 2020, and how to get your documents and money ready without falling for scams.

Many women in Nigeria run real businesses for years without registering them: a food stall, a tailoring shop, a hair salon, a small soap or zobo brand sold on WhatsApp. The business works, so why bother with forms? The simple answer is that **registration turns your hustle into something the law, banks and big customers can see and trust**. Without it, the business exists only in your head and your phone.

In Nigeria, businesses are registered by the **Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)**. The CAC keeps the official register of business names and companies under the **Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020 (CAMA 2020)**, the main law on business registration. When you register, the CAC gives you a certificate and a registration number. A business name gets a **BN number** and a company gets an **RC number**. Anyone can search the public register to confirm that your business is real.

What registration gives you
**Protection of your name.** Once your name is registered, another person cannot register the same name with the CAC.
**A business bank account.** Banks ask for CAC documents before opening an account in a business name, so customers can pay "Ada's Kitchen" instead of your personal account.
**Access to bigger customers.** Supermarkets, schools, hotels, companies and government agencies usually ask for CAC documents before they buy from you.
**Access to support.** Many grants, loans, trainings and programmes, including those linked to SMEDAN, ask for registration as proof that you are serious.
**A path to product approval.** NAFDAC asks for evidence of CAC registration before it will register a food, drink or cosmetic product.

What "compliance" means day to day

Compliance sounds like a big word, but for a small business it comes down to a short list of habits. You register correctly. You keep your registration up to date, which mainly means filing **annual returns** with the CAC each year and reporting changes such as a new address. You keep simple records of money in and money out. You register for tax and file what is required, even when the tax due is zero. And if you sell a regulated product, you get the right approval before you sell and you label it honestly.
Worked example: which bodies apply?

For example, Halima runs a small business in Kaduna. She makes groundnut oil and kuli-kuli, packs them in branded bottles and nylon packs, and sells to two supermarkets and on WhatsApp. She also wants a bank loan.
CAC: yes. She needs a registered business so the supermarkets can pay her business account and the bank can lend to the business.
Tax: yes. Once registered, she should confirm her Tax ID and keep records so she can file returns, even if her tax due is small.
NAFDAC: yes. Packaged groundnut oil and kuli-kuli are food products sold to the public, so each product needs NAFDAC registration before supermarket sale.
SON: no. Her products are food, which NAFDAC regulates, so SON certification does not apply to them.
SMEDAN and local government: optional support from SMEDAN; she checks her local government about any permit for her production space.
Halima's compliance list is CAC first, then Tax ID and records, then NAFDAC for each packaged product. Knowing the order stops her from paying for things in the wrong sequence.

The CAC registers several kinds of entities, but most women starting out choose between two: a **business name** and a **private company limited by shares** (often written "Ltd"). Choosing well saves money now and stress later, so take time to understand both.
Business name: you and your business are one

A business name is the trading name of a person (a **sole proprietor**) or a group of people (a **partnership**). Registering it tells the public who is behind "Ngozi Fabrics". It is simple and usually the cheapest option. But the law does not see the business as separate from you. If the business owes money, **you personally owe it**, and your own property can be used to pay. Income from the business is taxed as your personal income through your State Internal Revenue Service.
Limited company: a separate legal person

A private limited company is a **separate legal person**. It can own property, sign contracts, borrow money and be sued in its own name. The owners are **shareholders**, who hold **shares** in the company. The people who manage it are **directors**. One person can be both. The key benefit is **limited liability**: if the company fails, shareholders generally lose only what they put in, not their personal homes or savings, unless they signed personal guarantees or broke the law.
A balance scale
Weigh simplicity and low cost against protection and growth when you choose a structure.
What CAMA 2020 changed for small businesses
**One person can form a private company.** Under the old law you needed at least two people. Now a single shareholder who is also the director can register a company.
**Minimum share capital is low.** For a private company, CAMA 2020 sets the minimum issued share capital at 100,000 naira, at the time of writing.
**Small companies get lighter rules.** A small private company does not have to appoint a company secretary, and qualifying small companies can be exempt from having their accounts audited.
**Business names now file annual returns too.** CAMA 2020 brought annual returns for business names, not only companies.

Bisi: low risk, one person, small sales, no big contracts. A business name in her own name is enough for now.

Limited liability is not a free pass

If a director signs a personal guarantee for a loan, uses company money for herself, or trades fraudulently, she can still be held personally responsible. Keep company money separate from your own from the first day.

If you are unsure, ask yourself one question: if this business failed tomorrow and owed money, could I pay it from my own pocket without losing my home or savings? If the honest answer is no, and the risks are real, a limited company deserves serious thought even at an early stage.

There are other structures too, such as an incorporated trustee for churches, associations and NGOs, and a limited liability partnership for professionals. If your purpose is charitable or community work rather than profit, ask about incorporated trustees instead of a company.

Most registration delays happen before the form is even submitted: a name that gets rejected, a missing NIN, a blurry signature, or money paid to the wrong person. A little preparation turns a frustrating week into a smooth afternoon.
Choosing names that pass

The CAC first checks whether your proposed name is available. A name is usually refused if it is identical or too similar to an existing registered name, if it is offensive or misleading, or if it uses restricted words without approval. Words that suggest a link to government, such as **Federal, National, State or Government**, need consent. Words tied to regulated sectors, such as **Bank, Insurance or Microfinance**, need approval from the regulator of that sector.
Prepare **three options**, from your favourite to your back-up.
Make each name distinctive: add a local word, your own name, or a clear product word, such as "Amaka Okoro Kitchen" rather than "Good Food".
For a company, the name must end with "Limited" or "Ltd".

Budget and timeline

CAC fees, and the time it takes to approve applications, change from time to time. Always read the **current fee shown on the CAC portal at the point of payment**, and be wary of any website that quotes a fixed official price. A company costs more than a business name, and part of a company's cost depends on its share capital, because stamp duty is charged on it. If you use an agent, their professional fee is separate from the CAC fee, so ask for a written breakdown.
Worked example: planning a registration budget
For example, Esther in Ibadan has 60,000 naira set aside and wants a business name for her small bakery, with her first supermarket meeting in three weeks.
She logs into the CAC portal and notes the business name fee shown for her application, rather than trusting a figure from a blog.
She adds a small amount for data and printing, and a few thousand naira for passport photos.
She keeps the rest as a buffer in case her first name is rejected and she has to resubmit.
She starts the registration this week, because approval can take several working days and she wants the certificate before the meeting.
Esther's budget is based on the official figure on the day she pays, with a buffer, and her timeline leaves room for a rejected name.
Avoid registration scams

Pay CAC fees only through the official portal's payment page. Be careful with people on social media promising "same day CAC" for cash to a personal account, or asking for your NIN, BVN, bank PIN or OTP. The CAC will never need your bank PIN or OTP. If you use an agent, ask for their accreditation and check it on the CAC website, and insist that the business is registered in **your** name with **your** email.
Doing it yourself or paying for help

You can register a business name yourself if you are comfortable with forms on your phone. Paying an accredited agent makes more sense for a company, for partnerships with several owners, or if your time is worth more than the fee. Either way, you remain the owner, so read every page before it is submitted and keep copies of everything that was filed in your name.

Your NIN, photo, signature and address are valuable personal data. Send them only through the official portal or to an agent you have checked, never in an open WhatsApp group. After registration, keep copies of everything in one safe folder. You will learn to build that folder later in the course.

Each step depends on the one before it, so do not skip the name check.
**Create your account.** Sign up on the CAC portal with your own email address and phone number, then verify the email. Write your password somewhere safe.

**Check and reserve the name.** Choose business name registration, enter your first name option and the type of business. The system checks availability. If it is approved, you can proceed with that name. If not, try your next option.

**Fill the registration form.** Enter the business address, the nature of the business, the start date, and the details of each proprietor or partner: full name as on NIN, date of birth, contact and residential address.
**Upload documents.** Add each proprietor's passport photograph and signature image where requested, and confirm identity details against the NIN.
**Review before paying.** Check every spelling, especially your names and the business name. Errors after approval are harder and costlier to fix.
**Pay the fee on the portal.** Use the payment option on the portal and keep the receipt or payment reference.
**Track and respond.** Check your email and the portal dashboard. If the CAC raises a query, read it, correct exactly what is asked and resubmit.
**Download your documents.** When approved, download the certificate and registration details and save them in your compliance folder.
Writing a good "nature of business"

The nature of business tells the public and regulators what you do. A vague description like "general business" can cause a query and can confuse a bank or NAFDAC later. Write it in simple words that match what you actually sell, and include closely related activities you plan within the next year or two. For example: "Production, packaging and sale of snacks and soft drinks, and outdoor catering services."
Worked example: fixing a query

For example, Kemi in Abeokuta submitted a business name application for "Kemi's Hair Hub". Three working days later she received an email: the uploaded signature was not clear and her surname was spelt differently from her NIN record.
She reads the query carefully and notes the two problems: unclear signature, surname mismatch.
She signs again on clean white paper with a black pen, photographs it in daylight and crops it tightly.
She opens the application from her dashboard and corrects her surname to match the NIN exactly, letter for letter.
She uploads the new signature, resubmits, and saves a screenshot of the resubmission page.
Two days later the application is approved and she downloads her certificate.
Kemi fixed only what the query asked for, kept proof of resubmission, and got approval without paying again.

Registering a company asks you to make decisions that a business name does not: how many shares to create, who owns them, who will be a director, and what rules will govern the company. These decisions affect control, tax, cost and future investment, so make them with a pen and a calculator before you open the portal.
The main decisions
**Company name** ending in "Limited" or "Ltd", checked and reserved on the portal.
**Registered office address** in Nigeria where official letters can reach the company.
**Share capital**: the number of shares and their value. For a private company, CAMA 2020 sets a minimum issued share capital of 100,000 naira at the time of writing.
**Shareholders** and how many shares each holds.
**Directors**: at least one for a small private company; each must be an adult and give identity details.
**Persons with significant control (PSC)**: people who ultimately own or control a significant share, who must be disclosed.
**Objects of the company**: what the company is set up to do, in clear words.
**Memorandum and Articles of Association**: the founding document. The CAC portal offers standard model articles, which suit most small companies.

How shares translate into control

Shares are a simple way to divide ownership. If a company issues 1,000,000 shares of 1 naira each, its issued share capital is 1,000,000 naira. A person holding 600,000 of those shares owns 60 percent. Ownership affects voting at general meetings and who receives dividends. Stamp duty is charged on share capital at registration, so a bigger share capital costs more to register. Choose a figure you can justify, not the biggest number you can think of.
Worked example: splitting shares between sisters

For example, Chioma and her sister Adaeze in Enugu are registering "Ada & Chioma Catering Ltd". Chioma will run the business full time and put in 700,000 naira of equipment and cash. Adaeze will contribute 300,000 naira and help at weekends.
They choose an issued share capital of 1,000,000 naira, made of 1,000,000 ordinary shares of 1 naira each, matching their total contribution.
Chioma takes 700,000 shares (70 percent) and Adaeze takes 300,000 shares (30 percent).
Both sisters become directors so either can sign for the company, with a rule that payments above an agreed amount need both signatures.
Chioma, with 70 percent, is listed as a person with significant control; they check the portal for whether Adaeze's 30 percent also needs to be disclosed, and complete the PSC section accordingly.
They adopt the standard model articles and write a short private agreement on what happens if one sister wants to leave.
The share split reflects what each sister put in, control is clear, and both can sign. The company is registered with share capital the sisters can explain to a bank.

Compliance is not only paperwork. It is about making sure the people who buy from you are safe, are told the truth and have their information protected. That is also good business: trust is what brings customers back.
NAFDAC or SON?

**NAFDAC** (the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control) regulates food, drinks, packaged water, drugs, cosmetics, medical devices and chemicals. If you package any of these for sale to the public, the product needs NAFDAC registration and a NAFDAC number on the label. **SON** (the Standards Organisation of Nigeria) sets Nigerian Industrial Standards and certifies locally manufactured products that NAFDAC does not regulate, through its MANCAP certification scheme. A product is regulated by one or the other, not both.

Food, drink, cosmetic, chemical?

NAFDAC has a dedicated route for micro and small enterprises. Its published procedure for registering MSME products lists these main stages: apply on the NAFDAC website or through a state office, submit documents and pay, book a facility inspection at a date you choose, have samples taken for laboratory analysis during the inspection, and collect your certificate once the inspection and lab results are satisfactory. The same document gives a target of **90 working days** from application to certificate.

A food or cosmetic label should tell the buyer what the product is, what is in it, how much is in it, who made it and where, the NAFDAC number, the batch number, and the manufacturing and expiry dates. Never print a NAFDAC number you have not been given, and never copy another brand's number. Avoid health claims such as "cures typhoid" or "reduces sugar": claims like these need evidence and approval, and false claims mislead people who may be sick.

For example, Ifeyinwa in Owerri makes a pepper sauce. Her current sticker says "Ify's Hot Sauce, 100% natural, boosts immunity, NAFDAC approved". She has not yet applied to NAFDAC.
She removes "NAFDAC approved" immediately, because she has no NAFDAC number yet.
She removes "boosts immunity", a health claim she cannot prove.
She adds the ingredients in order of quantity, the net content (for example, 250 ml), her business name and address, and space for the NAFDAC number, batch number and dates.
She registers "Ify's Hot Sauce" as a business name, starts the trademark process, and prepares the MSME application documents.
Her label is now honest and ready for NAFDAC review, and she avoids the risk of having products seized for false claims.

The **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, enforced by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, protects personal information such as names, phone numbers, addresses and payment details. For a small business, follow simple rules: collect only what you need, tell customers why you are collecting it, do not add people to broadcast lists without their agreement, keep customer lists on a phone or account with a password, and never share someone's details with another business without their consent.

Registering a business name with the CAC protects the name on the business register, but it does not by itself protect a product brand or logo. Brand names and logos are protected as **trademarks**, through the Trademarks, Patents and Designs Registry under the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment. NAFDAC's MSME procedure lists trademark documentation among its requirements, so start the trademark process early.

Show clear prices and say upfront whether delivery is included.

If a customer reports a problem with a food or cosmetic product, record the batch number, stop selling that batch until you understand the problem, and respond respectfully.

Register the business in your own name, keep your own login details, and be a signatory on the business bank account. If a husband, partner or relative is a co-owner, write the share split and roles down. Clear records protect everyone and prevent disputes about who owns what.

Tax basics after the 2025 reforms

Nigeria's new tax laws took effect on 1 January 2026, so expect guidance to keep developing. At the time of writing, the main points for small businesses are these. A **company** files company income tax returns with the Nigeria Revenue Service. Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, a company that meets the legal definition of a **small company**, based on limits on its turnover and fixed assets, pays company income tax at **0 percent** and is excluded from the development levy, but it must still file. Check the current limits with the NRS, because definitions can be updated. A **business name** owner pays personal income tax on her business profit through her State Internal Revenue Service. **VAT** applies to many goods and services at 7.5 percent, but very small businesses below the legal threshold are not required to charge it. If you employ staff, you also deduct **PAYE** tax from their pay and remit it to the state.

Writing a short compliance statement

A compliance statement is a few honest sentences you can paste into an email, a WhatsApp message to a buyer, or a loan form. It says what is registered, what is up to date and what is in progress. Never claim something you do not have. Saying "NAFDAC application submitted" when it is true is far better than implying approval.
Worked example: a vendor registration message
For example, Funmi in Abeokuta wants to supply bottled zobo to a chain of three supermarkets. The purchasing officer asks for her details on WhatsApp.
She opens her compliance pack and picks the four documents asked for: CAC certificate, status report, NAFDAC certificate for the zobo, and a bank letter or account details.

She writes: "Good afternoon. Funmi Drinks Ltd (RC number on the attached certificate) is registered with the CAC and up to date with annual returns. Our zobo drink is NAFDAC registered (number on label and certificate attached). Payments go to our company account at the bank shown. Our Tax ID confirmation is attached."

In Nigeria, the Corporate Affairs Commission, the CAC, registers businesses under the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020, called CAMA 2020. Once your name is registered, nobody else can register it.

A business name is the trading name of a person or partnership. It is simple and usually cheapest. But the law sees you and the business as one. If the business owes money, you personally owe it.
A private limited company is a separate legal person. If it fails, shareholders generally lose only what they put in, not their homes or savings.
Under CAMA 2020, one person can form a company, and the minimum issued share capital is 100,000 naira, at the time of writing.

Chioma and her sister will sign catering contracts, with a risk of a large claim if food goes wrong. A limited company protects their personal property.
Funmi wants an investor for her drinks factory. An investor can only buy shares in a company, not a business name.

Tax basics
Company: files with the NRS
Small company: 0 percent tax, still files
Business name: personal tax via your state

Nigeria's new tax laws took effect on 1 January 2026, so guidance is still developing. A company files company income tax returns with the Nigeria Revenue Service.
A company that meets the legal definition of a small company pays 0 percent company income tax, but it must still file.
A business name owner pays personal income tax on profit through her State Internal Revenue Service.
Companies must keep accounting records for six years. Even when tax due is nothing, filing proves you are compliant and helps you get a tax clearance certificate.

Step by step
Building your compliance pack
Send any document a buyer or bank asks for the same day.
Create one main folder for the business
Add eight numbered section folders
Save clear PDFs, date first in the name
Keep a printed set of key documents
Put a one-page index at the front

A compliance pack is one organised folder holding every document that proves your business is registered, up to date and allowed to sell what it sells. Create one main folder, for example on Google Drive.
Inside, make eight numbered sections: registration, annual returns, tax, bank, product approvals, premises, records and people.
Scan each document clearly as a PDF, and name it with the date first, so files stay in order.
Keep a printed set of the most-requested documents in a plastic file at your business.
Add an index listing each document, its date, and its expiry or next due date. If a document is lost, the index makes replacement much faster.
Review it for ten minutes a month, and it is ready whenever a supermarket, bank or inspector asks.

A gap check before a loan

Tax ID never confirmed: confirm it

Records for 5 of 8 months: rebuild 3

Buyers and lenders care less about the certificate itself, and more about what it signals: that you are real, traceable and organised.
So never claim something you do not have.
Saying NAFDAC application submitted, when it is true, is far better than implying approval.

Safety first
Protect your pack and your money
Strong password, two-step verification, no documents in group chats.
A processing fee, your BVN and OTP, or an unofficial link means stop.
Check the repayment against your net profit. Read every term before signing.
Your pack holds ID numbers, signatures and bank details. Use a strong password and two-step verification. Send only the document asked for, marked for its purpose.

Be very careful with grant offers that ask for a processing fee, your BVN and OTP, or a link that is not on an official government domain. Real programmes, like those from SMEDAN, never ask for your PIN or OTP.
Before a loan, calculate the monthly repayment and check it against your monthly net profit. Read every term, and avoid personal guarantees you do not fully understand.
Schedule it
Every day: record sales and expenses
Month end: statement, summary, update pack
Once a year: CAC annual return
Once a year: tax return
Before expiry: renew certificates
Compliance becomes easy when it is scheduled. Every day, record sales and expenses. At month end, download your statement, write your summary and update the pack.
Once a year, file your CAC annual return and your tax return.
And renew certificates before they expire. Set two reminders for each: one month before, and one week before. Even with an accountant, you are the one responsible.
Days 1 to 30: register, start daily records
Days 31 to 60: Tax ID, business account
Days 61 to 90: fix label, apply to NAFDAC
Day 90: update pack, set reminders, review
For example, Esther runs a bakery in Ibadan with many gaps. In days 1 to 30, she registers her business name and starts daily records.
In days 31 to 60, she confirms her Tax ID, opens a business account, and moves all customer payments into it.
In days 61 to 90, she fixes her cookie label and applies to NAFDAC for one product.
At day 90, she updates her pack and sets reminders for her first annual return and tax filing.
If a task slips, give it a new date and a reason. An honest plan that is 80 percent done beats a perfect plan that hides gaps.
